lead: An actuator is the hand of the electronic control unit (ECU). The ECU computes a small electrical command; an actuator turns that command into force, motion or switching. Solenoids push or pull a plunger, relays and contactors switch heavy currents, and stepper motors move in precise angular steps. Drivers supply the current, diodes absorb inductive kickback, and PWM controls average current. You meet these devices in fuel injectors, exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) valves, variable valve timing, idle-air control and electric motor actuators. Some syllabi call them output devices.
prereq: You need: sensor basics and signal conditioning for signal levels and noise, basic transistors, diodes and magnetic circuits, and the ignition coil driver from the ignition systems topic.

sections.h3: Solenoids: current, force and the freewheeling diode

blocks.text: A solenoid is a coil with a movable iron plunger. Current in the coil creates a magnetic field; the field pulls the plunger into the coil. The pull force for an ideal magnetic circuit is
F ≈ μ<sub>0</sub> N² I² A / (2 g²)
blocks.where: F is force in newtons (N); μ<sub>0</sub> = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m; N is coil turns; I is coil current in A; A is pole face area in m²; g is air gap in m. The force rises with I² and falls quickly as g grows.

blocks.text: At switch-on the air gap is large, so the solenoid needs a pull-in current. After the plunger moves, a smaller hold current keeps it seated. The ECU uses pulse-width modulation (PWM):
I<sub>avg</sub> is average coil current in A; D is duty cycle from 0 to 1; V<sub>b</sub> is battery voltage in V; R<sub>c</sub> is coil resistance in Ω.

A low-side driver switches the coil's ground side with a MOSFET (metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor); a high-side driver switches the battery side. Both need a freewheeling diode across the coil. When the MOSFET turns off, coil current cannot stop instantly. The diode gives a path, so the stored energy ½ L I² is dissipated safely; L is coil inductance in henries and I is coil current in A. Without it, a high voltage spike can destroy the driver. Fuel injectors, EGR valves and variable valve timing units use this pattern. Ignition coil drivers use the same low-side switch, but deliberately without a freewheeling diode, because the inductive kick is what fires the spark; the switch is protected by other means. Spark generation belongs to ignition systems. A vacuum-operated actuator uses a small solenoid valve to switch vacuum to a diaphragm; the diaphragm then moves a flap or EGR valve.

sections.h3: Relays, contactors and H-bridge motor drive

blocks.text: A relay is an electromagnetic switch. The coil is a solenoid; its plunger closes or opens contacts. A small ECU current controls a much larger load current. The coil still needs a flyback diode, because the driver transistor sees the same inductive kick. A contactor is a heavy-duty relay for high current, often used for battery isolation or a powerful motor. Relay contacts are slow and wear; use a semiconductor driver when fast PWM is needed.

An H-bridge drives a DC motor in both directions. Four switches sit around the motor: two high-side and two low-side. Closing one high-side and the opposite low-side makes current flow one way; the other diagonal reverses it. Never close both switches on the same leg: that is shoot-through, a short circuit from battery to ground. Dead time between changes prevents it. PWM on the high-side switch sets average motor voltage V<sub>avg</sub> = D V<sub>b</sub>, so speed changes with duty cycle. H-bridges operate throttle actuators, EGR motor valves and other bidirectional motor actuators. A relay can reverse a motor only with extra contacts; an H-bridge does it electronically and quietly.

sections.h3: Stepper motors: steps, modes and limits

blocks.text: A stepper motor moves in fixed angular steps. The stator has several phase windings; the rotor is a permanent magnet or a soft-iron toothed rotor. The driver energises phases in sequence. Each change moves the rotor to the next stable position.

blocks.where: β is the step angle in degrees and S is the number of steps per revolution.

blocks.text: In full-step mode, one or two phases are on at a time; a 1.8° motor has 200 steps per revolution. Half-step mode alternates one-phase and two-phase states, giving 0.9°. Microstep mode applies sine and cosine currents to two phases. The rotor then settles between full-step positions; a driver may use 1/8, 1/16 or finer microsteps. Microstepping gives smoother motion and less vibration, but it does not increase holding torque. Holding torque is the torque needed to move the rotor from its energised position.

Stepper motors are open-loop. The ECU sends pulses and assumes the rotor follows. I<sub>f</sub> load torque is too high, or acceleration is too fast, the rotor slips and loses steps. There is no position feedback unless a sensor is added. Torque falls as speed rises because coil inductance limits how fast current can build; the driver needs a higher voltage to force current into the coil quickly. Pull-out torque is the maximum load torque at a given speed. Stepper actuators appear in idle-air control, headlamp levelling and some valve or flap positions.

spec.aria: Circuit: 12 volts, a 6 ohm coil with a diode across it, a MOSFET to ground switched by the ECU PWM output. Graph of coil current against time: a rise to 2 amps for pull-in, then a drop to a rippling 0.2 amp hold level.

examples.question: A stepper motor has a step angle of 1.8°. The ECU sends 400 steps in 0.8 s. Find the total angle turned, the number of revolutions and the average speed in rev/s and rpm.
steps: Step angle β = 1.8°. Number of steps n = 400. Total angle θ = n × β = 400 × 1.8 = 720°.
Average speed in rev/s = revolutions / time = 2 / 0.8 = 2.5 rev/s.
examples.answer: The motor turns 720° (2 revolutions) at an average speed of 2.5 rev/s, which is 150 rpm.
examples.check:
beta = 1.8
steps = 400
time_s = 0.8
angle_deg = steps * beta
rev = angle_deg / 360.0
speed_rps = rev / time_s
speed_rpm = speed_rps * 60.0
print(angle_deg)
print(rev)
print(speed_rps)
print(speed_rpm)

examples.question: A solenoid has N = 500 turns and a pole face of 1 cm². Using F ≈ μ₀N²I²A ÷ (2g²), find the pull at 1 A with a 1.0 mm air gap and with the plunger seated (0.2 mm gap). What current holds the seated plunger with the same pull as at pull-in? I<sub>f</sub> the coil is 6 Ω on 12 V, what PWM duty gives that hold current?
steps: Data in SI units: μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ = 1.2566 × 10⁻⁶ H/m, A = 1 × 10⁻⁴ m², N² = 250 000.
At g = 0.2 mm the gap term is 25 times smaller, so F = 15.7 × 25 = 393 N at the same 1 A.
Force goes as (I ÷ g)², so the same 15.7 N at 0.2 mm needs I = 1 × 0.2 ÷ 1.0 = 0.2 A.
Full-on current is 12 ÷ 6 = 2 A; with I<sub>avg</sub> ≈ D V<sub>b</sub> ÷ R<sub>c</sub>, a hold of 0.2 A needs D = 0.2 × 6 ÷ 12 = 0.10 (10 %).
Check on heat: the coil dissipates I²R = 2² × 6 = 24 W full on but only about 0.2² × 6 = 0.24 W at the hold current, which is why injectors and valves use peak-and-hold drive.
examples.answer: 15.7 N at 1.0 mm and 393 N at 0.2 mm (both at 1 A); 0.2 A holds the seated plunger with 15.7 N, which a 10 % PWM duty gives on 12 V.

traps: A relay coil and a solenoid coil are inductors: removing current without a freewheeling diode causes a high voltage spike and can destroy the driver.
Pull-in current is larger than hold current. Do not use the pull-in current for continuous holding; the coil overheats.
A stepper motor is open-loop. It can lose steps under overload or fast acceleration; counting pulses does not guarantee position.
In an H-bridge, switching both transistors on one leg at the same time causes shoot-through. Dead time is required.
Microstepping gives smoother motion, not more holding torque. The torque increment gained per microstep is smaller than for a full step; the motor's maximum holding torque stays the same.

quiz.q: Define step angle of a stepper motor.
quiz.a: Step angle β is the angle the rotor turns for one phase change; β = 360° / S, where S is steps per revolution.

quiz.q: State the function of a freewheeling diode across a solenoid coil.
quiz.a: It gives coil current a path when the driver turns off, limiting inductive voltage and protecting the driver.

quiz.q: Why does a solenoid need more current to pull in than to hold?
quiz.a: At pull-in the air gap is large, so magnetic force is weak; after the plunger moves, the small gap gives more force at lower current.

quiz.q: What is shoot-through in an H-bridge?
quiz.a: Shoot-through is both switches on one leg conducting together, shorting battery to ground; dead time prevents it.

quiz.q: A 1.8° stepper receives 250 steps. Find the angle turned and the number of revolutions.
A 12 V solenoid coil has R = 6 Ω and PWM duty 25%. Find average current, ignoring inductance.
Why can an open-loop stepper lose position at high speed?
quiz.a: Coil inductance limits current rise, so torque falls with speed. I<sub>f</sub> load torque or acceleration demand exceeds available torque, the rotor slips and pulses no longer match position.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production actuators increasingly integrate the driver, current sense and diagnostics into one smart module, often on a LIN bus. Engineers use model-based current control and high-side gate drivers with active clamping instead of a simple diode. Stepper and BLDC actuators compete in valve and headlamp applications. Search for smart actuators, peak-and-hold injector drivers, microstepping current control and ISO 26262 actuator diagnostics.
